messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omid was a 40-year-old paramedic who had dedicated his life to helping others, but the weight of a traumatic experience had begun to erode the very foundation of his being. The incident that haunted him occurred during a routine emergency call when he and his team responded to a car accident. Omid had witnessed the devastating injuries of a loved one, and the memory was now a relentless specter in his life. The sight of visible wounds, the anguished cries, and the smell of antiseptic lingered in his mind long after the chaos of that day had receded. Each time he encountered a similar scene at work, his heart raced, and he felt a wave of nausea wash over him. The triggers—visible injuries, reminders of victims, and the hospital smell—were inescapable, leading him to increasingly avoid work, which he had once embraced with passion.

In the months following the accident, Omid found himself caught in a cycle of avoidance. He started deliberately missing shifts, fearing he would be exposed to similar traumatic reminders. He told himself that it was better to stay home, to suppress the thoughts that clawed at him. Yet, this strategy only deepened his sense of failure, as he felt he was letting down his colleagues and the very people he aimed to protect. The internal conflict manifested in an increasing tendency to overwork when he was on duty, throwing himself into tasks to keep his mind occupied, hoping to forget the trauma. However, the more he tried to suppress his thoughts, the more they seemed to resurface with a vengeance, and he found himself in a relentless battle with the memories that would often ambush him, leaving him shaken and on edge.

Omid's daily life became riddled with anxiety. He started to react with alarm when touched unexpectedly—a colleague's friendly pat on the back would send him jumping, his heart racing as if he were still at the scene of the accident. It was as though an invisible wire had been pulled taut within him, ready to snap at the slightest provocation. He struggled to concentrate at work, his mind perpetually drifting back to that tragic day. Each time he attempted to focus on a patient, the memories would flood back in vivid detail, overwhelming him with the sensations he had experienced, the terror of being unable to save someone he cared for. The recollections came with an intensity that felt as real as the moment itself, leaving him breathless and terrified.

As Omid grappled with these intrusive memories, he began to internalize a narrative of failed protection. He believed that he had permanently changed for the worse, that he could no longer rely on himself to perform his duties effectively, and that he had failed in his role as a protector. This deep-seated belief not only magnified his sense of vulnerability but also made the triggers all the more potent. When he encountered a victim—whether in the field or in a hospital setting—he couldn't shake the guilt of having not done enough. The memories of that fateful day seemed to taunt him, reminding him of his perceived shortcomings.

The threat of reliving the trauma was an ever-present shadow in Omid's life. Each reminder of the accident heightened his anxiety, forcing him to grapple with the reality of what had happened, yet the memories felt fragmented. He often encountered gaps in his recollection, moments he simply could not grasp, which only fueled his frustration and exacerbated his feelings of inadequacy. Fearing that he might encounter the same chaos again, he sought out safe seats wherever he went, always choosing places where he felt more secure, yet this behavior only reinforced his belief that he was incapable of facing the world as he once had.

In this cycle of pain, Omid's maladaptive strategies became both a refuge and a prison. While avoiding situations that reminded him of the trauma offered brief reprieve, it ultimately left him feeling trapped and isolated. His relationships suffered; his wife noticed his withdrawal, and their conversations grew strained as he battled his inner demons alone. The realization that he was not the man he once was weighed heavily on him, and he found himself at a crossroads.

Now, as he sat in the therapist’s office, Omid felt a mix of fear and hope. He had finally taken the step to seek help, driven by a desperate desire to reclaim the life he had lost. What frightened him most was the thought of never being able to move past the trauma, of forever being haunted by the memories that had turned his world upside down. Yet, amid the fear, there was a flicker of hope—a hope that healing could lead him back to the man he used to be, someone capable of facing the world without the shadow of guilt and terror looming over him.
